meta.note: Chhath has no founder and no single book. The stories below are the ones most often told in Bihar. Another district will tell them another way, and that is all right.

intro.title: What we carry to the ghat
intro.subtitle: The stories behind Chhath, told the way we tell them in Bihar.
intro.paragraph: Chhath is four days in Kartik, and most of it happens at the river. The rest is memory: a few old stories that families carry down to the ghat along with the soop and the sugarcane. These are the ones we tell.

facts.label: The sixth day
facts.text: Chhath is named for the sixth day of the waxing moon in Kartik.

facts.label: Two offerings
facts.text: Sandhya Arghya to the setting sun, Usha Arghya to the rising one.

facts.label: No priest
facts.text: The ghat is the temple. The vrati is the one who keeps the fast.

chapters.title: The sun we can see

image.alt: A geometric Surya mandala with the sun god at its centre, surrounded by planetary attendants
image.caption: A Surya mandala, Rajasthan, c. 18th century. The sun sits at the centre of the planetary orbits.

body: Long before any temple, there was the river and the sun. In Bihar the sun is not a picture in a book. It comes up over the Ganga, dries the paddy spread out on the road, and goes down behind the same water in the evening. We see it every day. Maybe that is why we can stand in front of it and hold up water.
Arghya is just that: water in both hands, a few flowers, a little rice. The sun takes it from everyone the same way.
chapters.note: Surya is called Pratyaksha Devta, the god you can see.

inset.alt: Vintage chromolithograph of Surya standing on a seven-horse chariot inside a blazing golden orb
inset.caption: Surya on his seven-horse chariot. Ravi Varma Press chromolithograph.

chapters.title: The son who did not forget

image.alt: Pahari painting of Karna seated in a golden chariot on the battlefield of Kurukshetra
image.caption: Karna in his chariot at Kurukshetra, from a Pahari-school Mahabharata series.

body: Karna is the one we tell first. His mother was Kunti, still a girl when she called on the sun god and was given a son. She could not keep him. She put him in a basket and set it on the river, and a charioteer named Adhiratha found the child and raised him.

He grew up to be king of Anga, the land around Bhagalpur and Munger. He had little to thank the world for. Still, every morning before he went to court, he stood in the Ganga and offered water to his father.
People here say that is how Chhath began in Bihar. Not from a book. From a son who did not forget.
chapters.note: Anga is the old name for the Bhagalpur and Munger belt.

chapters.title: Draupadi in the forest

image.alt: Ravi Varma Press print of Draupadi seated with the five Pandavas under a royal canopy
image.caption: Draupadi with the Pandavas. Ravi Varma Press, c. 1910.

body: The Pandavas had lost their kingdom and were living in the forest. Draupadi had nothing left to give. The sage Dhaumya told her to worship the sun. She kept the fast of Kartik and stood in the water with her offering. After that, things changed for the Pandavas. They won the kingdom back.
In Ranchi, in Nagdi village, women still go to a spring instead of the river. They say that is where she stood.
chapters.note: Nagdi is one of the few Chhath ghats that is not on a river.

chapters.title: Sita comes home

image.alt: Kalighat painting of Rama, Sita and Lakshmana travelling home on a swan boat
image.caption: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana return to Ayodhya. Kalighat school, 19th century.

body: After fourteen years in the forest, Ram and Sita came back to Ayodhya. Ram had killed Ravana, and the priests told him he must atone. In Mithila they say Sita kept the fast of Kartik Shashthi and offered water for that atonement.
In Munger there is a rock in the middle of the Ganga with her footprint on it. In Janakpur, where she was born, Chhath is the day a daughter comes home.
chapters.note: The rock is called Sita Charan. It sits in the river at Munger.

chapters.title: The sixth day

image.alt: Colourful folk murti of the goddess Shashthi holding a child, seated on a cat
image.caption: Shashthi with the child Skanda. Folk murti from Bagbazar, Kolkata.

body: There was a king called Priyavrat and a queen called Malini. They had no child. They performed the yagya for a son, and a bowl of kheer rose out of the fire. The queen ate it and became pregnant.

The child was born dead. Malini ran to the river to end her life. A woman stopped her at the water and said: I am Devasena, the sixth. Worship me and the sun, and you will have a child. Malini did, and she was blessed.
That is Chhathi Maiya, the sixth form of Prakriti, the one who looks after children. In Bihar nobody calls her Shashthi. She is Maiya, the mother.
Women fast for their children. Then the children grow up and fast for their mother. You will see both at the same ghat, keeping the same fast.
chapters.note: The story is told in the Brahmavaivarta Purana. Shashthi is also worshipped six days after a child is born.

chapters.title: Why here

image.alt: Women in orange and red saris holding bamboo soops filled with fruit and flowers at a Chhath ghat
image.caption: Offerings of the first harvest, carried to the water in bamboo soops.

body: By Kartik the rains are over and the water has come down. The fields are full. The first rice, the sugarcane, the coconut and the thekua go to the river before anyone eats them.

Chhath is the one festival where no priest is needed. The family keeps the fast, the family carries the daura, the family stands in the water. That is why it travels so well. From Patna to Janakpur to New Jersey, it is still done at home.
chapters.note: The fast begins on Kartik Shukla Chaturthi and ends with Usha Arghya.

inset.alt: Historic photograph of the stone Sun Temple at Deo in Aurangabad district, Bihar
inset.caption: The Sun Temple at Deo, Aurangabad — Bihar's own house of Surya. Photograph, 1860s.

epilogue.title: The sun goes. The sun comes back.

image.alt: Clay lamps and offerings glowing on a Chhath ghat after dark, reflected in the river
image.caption: Lamps and offerings on the ghat through the night.

body: On Sandhya Arghya we offer to the sun as it goes down. Then the night on the ghat: lamps, songs, cardamom tea, somebody's baby asleep on a blanket, somebody's mother asleep sitting up.
At dawn the same sun comes back and the same hands lift the same soop. We offer water again.
For one night we wait for the sun to return. It always does. That is what we are thanking it for.

gallery.caption: Janakpur, where Sita was born. The Bagmati fills up for Chhath.

gallery.caption: Thekua. Wheat, jaggery and ghee, made a few days before.

gallery.alt: Bamboo soops, bananas, coconuts and clay lamps arranged on the ground for Chhath
gallery.caption: Soop, sugarcane, coconut, and the first of the harvest.

gallery.alt: Three women in red and yellow saris standing in the Yamuna river during Chhath in Delhi
